    Get started

    get-started.Rmd

    Introduction

    Goals of CheckrefR

    CheckrefR pursues two complementary goals.

    An R client for GROBID

    GROBID (GeneRation Of BIbliographic Data) is a machine learning model able to read a document (typically a PDF of a scientific article) or a list of raw references, and to extract structured information from it: title, authors, year, journal, DOI, etc.

    GROBID works as a service: a program that runs somewhere (on your computer or on a server) and to which you send files in order to get a result. CheckrefR plays the role of the client: it sends your files to the service, retrieves the response and turns it into R tables that are ready to use.

    Two usage modes are available:

    Mode Principle When to use it?
    Local ("docker") GROBID runs on your machine, in a Docker container (an isolated “box” that bundles the program). Recommended: fast, private, no volume limit.
    Remote ("remote") Files are sent to a GROBID server accessible over the Internet. Troubleshooting, first trials, or if you have your own server.

    ⚠️ Keep in mind. The remote servers configured by default in the package are demonstration servers: shared, sometimes unavailable or slow, and with no guarantee of confidentiality for your documents.

    It is preferable to use GROBID locally or to have your own server. The package lets you configure the server address (see grobid_remote_connect() below).

    The package also offers a route that is independent of GROBID: the parse_apa_text() function, based on regular expressions, which parses references in APA 7 format. Its output can then be validated with the same pipeline.

    Verification of bibliographic references

    The second part of the package consists in checking that bibliographic references really exist and that they are correctly described. The references extracted by GROBID are compared against the open database OpenAlex and/or against DOI resolution (doi.org).

    Why verify? The context of generative AI

    CheckrefR was designed in particular with the context of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in mind. Large language models (LLMs) can produce bibliographies that look perfectly credible, but whose quality varies greatly. In general, one may encounter:

    • outright hallucinations: the reference does not exist (invented title, authors and journal);
    • exact references: the reference exists and all of its information is correct;
    • approximate references: a real work, but with errors (year, authors, distorted title, incorrect journal);
    • hallucinated DOIs attached to a real reference: the reference text matches a real article, but the DOI is wrong or points to another publication;
    • the opposite: a real DOI attached to an erroneous reference;
    • ambiguous cases, where the reference is partially correct and it is difficult to decide.

    This diversity is what makes it necessary to perform a verification that goes beyond a simple “the DOI exists / does not exist”, and that compares all the elements (title, authors, year, DOI).

    ⚠️ Warning: experimental version

    • The current version of the package is experimental.
    • The computation of matching scores (title, authors, year, global score) is currently the subject of more thorough work and preparation than the method presently implemented, which has limitations.
    • More formal tests on this question will be carried out in the future.
    • Statuses and scores should therefore be read as decision aids and not as a verdict: manual verification remains necessary, especially for ambiguous or partially correct cases.

    Prerequisite: installing Docker (local mode)

    The local mode, recommended above, relies on Docker. This is software that runs programs in isolated “boxes” (containers), without installing anything else on your machine. GROBID is distributed in this form: Docker is therefore needed only if you wish to use it locally. Without Docker, the remote mode remains available (see the caveats above).

    🐳 Installing Docker according to your system

    • Windows: install Docker Desktop. It relies on WSL 2, which the installer offers to enable. A restart may be requested.
    • macOS: install Docker Desktop, choosing the version suited to your processor (Apple Silicon or Intel).
    • Linux: install Docker Engine via your distribution’s package manager (Debian/Ubuntu, Fedora/RHEL…), start the service, and add your user to the docker group to avoid using sudo.

    See the official documentation.

    grobid_check_requirements() tells you whether it is detected, and grobid_install_guide() provides instructions adapted to your system (see below).

    Getting GROBID up and running

    Overview

    Getting started takes place in three steps:

    1. Diagnose your environment: grobid_check_requirements();
    2. Install if necessary, with an interactive guide: grobid_install_guide();
    3. Start GROBID, locally with grobid_docker_start() or by connecting to a remote server with grobid_remote_connect().

    Once GROBID is available, documents are processed with grobid_process_file() and grobid_process_files() (next section).

    Step 1: check your environment with grobid_check_requirements()

    This function diagnoses your system: operating system, Internet access, presence and state of Docker, any active GROBID container, and accessibility of the default remote servers. It then recommends a usage mode.

    req <- grobid_check_requirements()
#> ℹ Checking Internet connection...
#> ✔ Internet reachable (via Google).
#> 
#> ── Testing remote servers ──
#> 
#> ℹ Testing <https://grobidorg-grobid.hf.space> [crf]...

#> ℹ Testing <https://grobidorg-grobid2.hf.space> [crf]...
#> ℹ Testing <https://grobidorg-grobid-full.hf.space> [full]...
#> ℹ Testing <https://grobidOrg-grobid-full2.hf.space> [full]...
#> ℹ Checking Docker...
#> 
#> ── GROBID Diagnostic ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>

    The result is also returned (invisibly) as a list:

    req$recommended_mode
#> [1] "docker"

    The recommended value is "docker" if Docker is installed, and "remote" if Docker is absent but a remote server responds.

    Argument Role
    check_docker Checks Docker and any active GROBID container.
    check_remote Tests the default remote servers.
    test_all_urls TRUE: tests all addresses; FALSE: stops at the first one that responds (faster).
    verbose Displays (or not) the diagnosis in the console. 
    # Silent diagnosis, without testing Docker
req <- grobid_check_requirements(verbose = FALSE, check_docker = FALSE)
req$recommended_mode

    Step 2: get guided through installation with grobid_install_guide()

    If Docker is not installed, grobid_install_guide() displays a step-by-step guide adapted to your system, then invites you to rerun the diagnosis. It is the interactive version of the box in the previous section.

    # Uses the previous diagnosis (otherwise, it is rerun automatically)
grobid_install_guide(requirements = req)
#> 
#> ── GROBID installation guide ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 
#> ── 1. Environment summary ──
#> 
#> • OS : windows (Windows mingw32)
#> • Internet : ✓
#> • Docker installed : ✓
#> • Docker running : ✗
#> • Remote server(s) reachable : ✓
#> ℹ Remote server found (fallback only): <https://grobidorg-grobid.hf.space> (mode: crf)
#> ✔ Mode "crf": 1 reachable server(s).
#> ✔ Mode "full": 1 reachable server(s).
#> 
#> ── 2. Recommended option ──
#> 
#> ✔ Docker is installed on this system: local mode is strongly recommended.
#> ℹ Docker is not currently running, but it can be started automatically. Run `grobid_docker_start()` - the package will attempt to start the Docker daemon and the GROBID container for you.
#> ! A remote server is reachable (mode: crf), but it should only be used as a temporary fallback (e.g. `grobid_remote_connect()`). Relying on Docker locally avoids depending on third-party service availability, rate limits, or downtime.
#> 
#> ── 3. Starting Docker ──
#> 
#> • Open the Docker Desktop application from the Start menu.
#> • Wait until the Docker icon in the taskbar is active.
#> • Restart R and run `grobid_install_guide()`, or directly
#> `grobid_docker_start()`.
#> 
#> ── 4. Validation test ──

    Step 3: start GROBID

    Two options, depending on the chosen mode.

    Local mode: grobid_docker_start()

    This function launches GROBID in a Docker container on your machine.

    grobid_docker_start()

    First launch: downloading the image. The first time, the GROBID model image (the “package” containing the program and its models) has to be downloaded to your machine, which can take a while (several GB). This is also the case for each new model or new version that has not yet been downloaded. Subsequent launches are much faster.

    Available settings:

    Argument Role Default value
    model_type Model used: "crf" (lightweight) or "full" (deep learning, more accurate but heavier) not set (standard image)
    grobid_version GROBID version "0.9.0"
    port Local port on which the service is exposed 8070
    max_ram Maximum memory allocated (e.g. "4g", "8g") "4g"
    pull Forces download/update of the image FALSE
    timeout_ready Maximum waiting time before GROBID is ready 120 s
    docker_image Base name of the Docker image "lfoppiano/grobid:"
    verbose Progress messages TRUE 
    # Full model, more memory, custom port
grobid_docker_start(model_type = "full", max_ram = "8g", port = 8080)

# Another GROBID version
grobid_docker_start(grobid_version = "0.8.1")

    If a compatible container (same image, version, model and port) is already active, it is simply reused; otherwise, it is replaced.

    Remote mode: grobid_remote_connect()

    This function tests and then stores a remote GROBID server for the current R session.

    # Default demonstration servers (crf model)
grobid_remote_connect()
    Argument Role
    url Address of your own GROBID server. If provided, model_type is ignored.
    model_type "crf" or "full": chooses among the default demonstration servers.
    timeout Maximum connection delay (120 s by default).
    verbose Progress messages. 
    # Your own server (recommended if you do not use Docker)
grobid_remote_connect(url = "https://mon-serveur-grobid.exemple.org")

# Demonstration servers, "full" model
grobid_remote_connect(model_type = "full")

    Reminder. The default servers are demonstration servers: avoid sending sensitive or large documents to them.

    These two functions are optional

    You can skip this step 3. grobid_docker_start() and grobid_remote_connect() are useful for fine-tuning the configuration (memory, port, version, personal server), but calling them manually is not required.

    The processing functions grobid_process_file() and grobid_process_files() call them on their own: you only need to specify the mode ("docker" or "remote") and the model_type ("crf" or "full"). If the server is not already active, it is then started or reached automatically.

    Processing documents with GROBID

    The grobid_process_file() and grobid_process_files() functions

    • grobid_process_file() processes a single file;
    • grobid_process_files() processes several files (optionally in parallel) and gathers the results into a single table.

    Main parameters:

    Argument Role
    file / files Path(s) of the file(s) to process.
    service Type of GROBID processing (see below).
    params Additional options passed to GROBID, e.g. list(consolidateCitations = 1).
    output_format "parsed" (R table, default) or "raw" (raw XML).
    output_dir Folder where XML files are saved (optional).
    mode "docker" or "remote": automatically starts or connects the server if necessary.
    model_type "crf" or "full": model used.
    parallel, n_workers (grobid_process_files()) parallel processing.
    on_error (grobid_process_files()) "warn" (continues) or "stop".

    Available services:

    service Input Extracted content
    "processFulltextDocument" PDF Structured full text and references
    "processHeaderDocument" PDF Header (title, authors, abstract…)
    "processReferences" PDF List of bibliographic references
    "processCitationList" .txt file or vector of texts Parsing of raw references (one per line)

    Illustration with the example file ref_test.txt

    The package provides a test file in its extdata folder. It contains a list of raw references, which can be processed with the "processCitationList" service.

    txt_file <- system.file("extdata", package = "CheckrefR") |>
  list.files(pattern = "ref_test", full.names = TRUE)

basename(txt_file)
#> [1] "ref_test.txt"

    readLines(txt_file, warn = FALSE) |>
  head(6) |> writeLines(sep = "\n\n")

    Processing the file

    Here, the mode and the model are specified directly: the server is started or reached automatically, without any prior call to grobid_docker_start() or grobid_remote_connect().

    refs <- grobid_process_file(
  file = txt_file,
  service = "processCitationList",
  mode = "docker",        # or "remote"
  model_type = "crf",
  output_format = "parsed"
)

    The result is a table (tibble) with one row per reference:

    dim(refs)
#> [1] 14 17
names(refs)
#>  [1] "ref_n"            "raw_reference"    "title"            "authors"         
#>  [5] "authors_list"     "year"             "journal"          "publisher"       
#>  [9] "volume"           "issue"            "pages"            "doi"             
#> [13] "pmid"             "url"              "ref_type"         "parse_confidence"
#> [17] "source_file"
    refs |>
  select(ref_n, title, authors, year, journal, doi) |>
  head(8) |>
  kable_site(caption = "References extracted by GROBID (preview)") |>
  column_spec(2, width = "22em")

    For several files, use grobid_process_files(), which adds a source_file column to identify the origin of each row. Example with any PDFs available in the package:

    pdf_files <- system.file("extdata", package = "CheckrefR") |>
  list.files(pattern = "\\.pdf$", full.names = TRUE)

refs_pdf <- grobid_process_files(
  files = pdf_files,
  service = "processReferences",
  mode = "docker",
  output_format = "parsed"
)

    Validating references

    Once the references are extracted, their existence and accuracy can be checked.

    Comparing against OpenAlex: validate_references()

    validate_references() takes the reference table as input (at minimum the columns title, authors_list, doi, year, ref_n, source_file) and follows a multi-step procedure:

    1. checking DOIs against OpenAlex;
    2. for unresolved or inconsistent DOIs, querying doi.org;
    3. if necessary, searching by title;
    4. computing matching scores (title, authors, year) and a global score;
    5. keeping one to max_candidates candidates per reference (3 by default).
    
checkrefr_set_defaults(oa_api_key = keyring::key_get("openalex"))

cache_file <- "validated_refs_2.rds"

if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
  results <- readRDS(cache_file)
} else {
  ref_path <- system.file("extdata", "ref_test.txt", package = "CheckrefR")
  results <- validate_references(refs, verbose = FALSE)
  saveRDS(results, cache_file)
}

    Main columns of the result:

    Column Content
    input_title, input_doi, input_year, input_authors Information of the reference as extracted.
    oa_title, oa_doi, oa_year, oa_authors Information of the candidate OpenAlex record.
    score_title, score_authors, score_year Similarity scores (0 to 1).
    score_global Weighted score: 60% title, 30% authors, 10% year.
    n_candidates Number of candidates retained for this reference.
    match_status Matching status (see below). 
    results |>
  select(ref_n, input_title, oa_title, score_title, score_authors,
         score_year, score_global, match_status) |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("score_"), ~ round(.x, 2))) |>
  head(10) |>
  kable_site(caption = "Validation results (preview)") |>
  column_spec(c(2, 3), width = "16em")

    Most frequent statuses:

    match_status Meaning
    confirmed_with_doi DOI confirmed, with matching title and year.
    partial_with_doi DOI found, but only a partial match.
    doi_mismatch The DOI exists, but designates another publication.
    doi_not_found DOI not found or nonexistent.
    title_search Match found through a title search.
    no_match No sufficiently close candidate. 
    results |>
  count(match_status, name = "n_lignes", sort = TRUE) |>
  kable_site(caption = "Distribution of matching statuses")
    Distribution of matching statuses
    match_status n_lignes
    title_search 17
    doi_does_not_exist 5
    no_match 4
    confirmed_with_doi 2
    doi_mismatch 2

    The thresholds (minimum score of 0.60; “probable” match from 0.85; DOI confirmation with a title score of at least 0.90 and an identical year) are those of the experimental version. See the warning in the introduction.

    Keeping the best match: deduplicate_references()

    Since validate_references() can return several candidates per reference, deduplicate_references() keeps only the best row (highest global score) for each source_file / ref_n pair. The order of the references is preserved.

    best <- deduplicate_references(results, verbose = TRUE)
    best |>
  select(ref_n, input_title, oa_doi, score_global, match_status) |>
  mutate(score_global = round(score_global, 2)) |>
  kable_site(caption = "One row per reference (best match)") |>
  column_spec(2, width = "22em")

    Alternative without GROBID: APA 7 format references

    For references already written in APA 7 (Authors (year). Title. Journal, volume(issue), pages. DOI), parse_apa_text() parses them using regular expressions, without a GROBID server. The as_ref_df = TRUE option produces a table directly compatible with validate_references().

    txt_files <- system.file("extdata", package = "CheckrefR") |>
  list.files(pattern = "\\.txt$", full.names = TRUE)

apa  <- txt_files[2]

    This method assumes a strictly compliant format: year in the form (YYYY), title ending at the first period following the year, DOI as a doi.org URL at the end of the reference. Non-compliant references may produce missing values or partial extractions, without any error message.
